newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. warn Bosnians of sanctions on refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warn Bosnians of sanctions on refugees.

text.p: The United States warned Bosnia's factions on Thursday they could face U.N. sanctions if they failed to restore freedom of movement in their ethnically divided country.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher issued the warning as Bosnia's three co-presidents met foreign ministers of major powers in Paris to approve a two-year plan intended to stabilise fragile peace in the former Yugoslav republic.

"We have made it clear to the parties that the Security Council will consider imposing measures if they fail to significantly meet their obligations under the peace agreement," Christopher told the conference.
He said Bosnians would be under close scrutiny regarding freedom of movement and the return of refugees.
International aid would also depend on the implementation of the agreement, including handing over suspects to the war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders elected in September were to pledge to set up joint institutions, enable the return of some two million refugees, ensure freedom of movement and freedom of the press, and build a market economy over two years.
In return, the international community will agree at the one-day conference to continue assistance in rebuilding Bosnia's administration and economy after nearly four years of war.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told the meeting aid would depend on Bosnians setting up a government before a second conference scheduled in London next month.
"We had some good progress but a lot of work remains to be done to reunite the country," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on arrival at the Kleber conference centre.

However, officials said a widely expected decision to keep an international military presence in Bosnia when the mandate of the NATO-led Peace Implementation Force (IFOR) expires at the end of the year will be taken only after further deliberation at NATO headquarters in Brussels, and not discussed in Paris.

Christopher met the Bosnian co-presidents on the eve of the talks and said the implementation of the Dayton peace agreement, signed a year ago, was at a "very critical stage" after a clash on Tuesday in which two Moslem refugees were killed.
"I urge all the people in Bosnia to avoid the kind of incident that took place (on Tuesday). That is not constructive and can only harm efforts to advance peace there," he said.
Christopher pressed Moslem Alija Izetbegovic, Serb Momcilo Krajisnik and Croat Kresimir Zubak to implement fully the Dayton peace accord.
He singled out the return of refugees, the holding of municipal elections and building a more active international police force as key issues.
A senior U.S. official held late-night talks with the three leaders to try to help them thrash out a joint cabinet list, but Bosnian officials said little progress was made.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, co-chairing the conference with international mediator Carl Bildt, told reporters the aim was to lay the foundations of a "moral contract" between the international community and Bosnia.
He said the rival factions must also cooperate more fully with the international tribunal in bringing wanted war criminals to justice. Only a handful have been handed over so far.

A French draft of the proposed declaration obtained by Reuters calls for Bosnia to pledge to have a working cabinet, parliament, central bank, constitutional court and military committee by next March at the latest.

A second conference in London in December will adopt a more detailed action programme for the next year, by which time NATO is likely to have formally approved a slimmed-down peacekeeping force to succeed IFOR.

Countries attending Thursday's talks were Bosnia- Herzegovina, Croatia and rump Yugoslavia, the United States, Russia, France, Britain, Germany, Italy, Canada, the Netherlands, Ireland as current president of the European Union and Turkey, representing the Islamic Conference Organisation.
